branching-merging.summary: Branches are cheap pointers; merging combines histories with a three-way merge from the best common ancestor. Know when Git fast-forwards, how strategies differ from strategy options, and how to resolve each kind of conflict.
points: A branch is a ref holding one commit hash; HEAD normally points at the current branch. Creating or deleting a branch copies or deletes no files.
A merge fast-forwards when HEAD is an ancestor of the merged commit. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit; `--ff-only` refuses anything but a fast-forward; `merge.ff` sets the default.
ort (default since Git 2.34) does a three-way merge against the merge base; with several bases it builds a virtual ancestor.
`-s ours` keeps your tree exactly and records the other branch as merged. `-X ours`/`-X theirs` only pick a side for conflicting hunks. There is no `-s theirs`.
`--squash` stages the combined changes with no merge parent, so `branch -d` refuses and later merges of the same branch can re-conflict.
During a merge, "ours" is HEAD and "theirs" is the merged branch. During a rebase they swap: "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto.
Resolve conflicts, `git add` each path, then `git merge --continue`. Set `merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3` to see the base, and enable rerere to reuse resolutions.
traps: Treating `-X ours` and `-s ours` as the same: one breaks ties, the other throws away the whole other side.
Expecting `git checkout --ours` to mean "my branch" during a rebase.
Assuming a clean merge means working code: semantic conflicts merge without markers, so build and test the merge result.
